text: This chapter has built up three separate ways of running the exact same Bell-state circuit, each revealing a different layer of truth. The real skill this lab builds isn't running any one of these — it's correctly diagnosing which deviations are real hardware effects and which are just sampling noise you'd see even on perfect hardware.

All three use the identical circuit: H on qubit 0, CX entangling it with qubit 1. Run (a), the noiseless statevector, gives exact P(00) and P(11) at 0.5, with no sampling at all. Run (b), noiseless shots at 1024, gave 00: 503, 11: 521, with 01 and 10 at zero. Run (c), noisy shots at 4096 with a 1% depolarizing CX error, gave 00: 2090, 01: 11, 10: 8, 11: 1987.

Compare (a) to (b). Both of run (b)'s outcomes, 00 and 11, were already possible under the exact result — only their split deviated slightly from 50/50. Run (b)'s simulator had zero noise model attached, so there's no hardware-error explanation available at all. It has to be sampling noise, and a 503/521 split at 1024 shots is well within the expected spread — no diagnostic alarm to raise.

Now look at run (c). The 01 and 10 counts are 11 and 8 — small, but not zero. This cannot be sampling noise alone, because run (a) establishes those probabilities are exactly zero under the ideal circuit. There is no number of noiseless shots that would ever produce a nonzero count there. Their appearance is only explained by the real depolarizing error — the signature of hardware-driven error: an outcome the ideal logic rules out entirely, showing up anyway.

The practical rule: before concluding a surprising count reflects a real physical effect, ask whether a noiseless simulation of the same circuit could plausibly produce that same deviation through sampling noise alone. An already-possible outcome with a modest deviation usually is just sampling noise. But an outcome the ideal circuit rules out entirely, showing up at all, is a real signal — it can't be explained away, because shot noise on a truly zero-probability outcome can never produce a nonzero count.
Chapter 4 turns these same counts dictionaries into something easier to read at a glance, starting with plot_histogram and the other visualization tools Qiskit gives you for communicating results.
